q: what is the effect of caffeine on sleep
how much caffeine is in coffee
a: Caffeine is a natural stimulant found in coffee beans, tea leaves, cacao, and kola nuts, and it's the world's most widely consumed psychoactive substance. It works by blocking adenosine receptors in the brain — adenosine is a neurotransmitter that promotes sleepiness, so blocking it keeps you alert and reduces fatigue. Caffeine also increases dopamine and norepinephrine, improving mood, focus, and reaction time. Its effects peak about 30-60 minutes after consumption and it has a half-life of roughly 5-6 hours, meaning half the caffeine is still in your system after that time — which is why caffeine late in the day can disrupt sleep. Moderate intake (up to about 400 mg/day, roughly 3-4 cups of coffee) is generally considered safe for healthy adults, but excessive amounts can cause anxiety, jitters, insomnia, and heart palpitations, and tolerance builds with regular use.

q: what does stress do to the body
how does stress affect the body
how does stress affect the heart
a: Stress is the body's physiological and psychological response to demands or threats, driven by the fight-or-flight response — the sympathetic nervous system releases adrenaline and cortisol, raising heart rate, blood pressure, and blood sugar while redirecting blood to muscles. Short-term (acute) stress is adaptive and can boost focus and performance, but chronic stress — when the response stays activated for weeks or months — takes a serious toll: it increases the risk of heart disease and high blood pressure, weakens the immune system, disrupts sleep and digestion, and contributes to anxiety and depression. Cortisol, the main stress hormone, also affects memory and metabolism. Managing stress involves regular exercise, adequate sleep, mindfulness and breathing techniques, social connection, and reducing known stressors.
